summary: Specifies Pragmatic General Multicast (PGM), a reliable multicast transport protocol. A receiver in the group either gets all the data, including repairs, or learns that some loss could not be recovered. It is an experimental specification.

plainLanguage.summary: When one person talks to a huge crowd, someone may miss a sentence. This is a way for people to ask for just the missed part again, or at least know they missed it.

questions: how does pgm handle lost packets
what is a nak in pgm
subtitle: Reliable multicast built on negative acknowledgments, with the network helping to deliver and confirm repair requests.

tldr.problem: Making multicast reliable the usual way, with positive acknowledgments from every receiver, overwhelms the source as the group grows (ACK implosion).
tldr.mechanism: PGM drops positive acknowledgments. Receivers send negative acknowledgments (NAKs) for missing packets, network elements forward and confirm them hop by hop, and repairs are sent only to the parts of the tree that missed the data.
tldr.outcome: A receiver either gets all the data, including repairs, or can detect that some loss could not be recovered. PGM is not meant for applications needing acknowledged delivery to a known group or total ordering among sources. It is an Experimental specification.

facts.label: Recommended GSI
facts.value: low-order 48 bits of MD5 of source DNS name

today: RFC 3208 is an Experimental specification and, in the data given here, is neither obsoleted nor updated. It does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.

sections.title: Goals and Guarantees
sections.content:
Pragmatic General Multicast (PGM) is a reliable multicast transport protocol for applications that need ordered or unordered, duplicate-free delivery from multiple sources to multiple receivers. It is meant for applications with basic reliability needs, not for sophisticated ordering or agreement requirements. Its central design goal is simplicity of operation with due regard for scalability and network efficiency.

The guarantee is carefully worded: a receiver in the group either receives all data packets from transmissions and repairs, or is able to detect unrecoverable data packet loss. PGM has no notion of group membership, and members may join and leave at any time. It is not intended for applications that depend on acknowledged delivery to a known group, or on total ordering among multiple sources.

The design avoids positive acknowledgments because ACK implosion keeps ACK-based reliable multicast from scaling. Instead the source uses timeouts to manage its transmit resources, and negative acknowledgments alone drive repairs. Without ACKs and group knowledge, the RFC admits, a receiver may still detect a loss too late for repair. PGM does not address conference control, global ordering among sources, or recovery from network partitions.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of everyone saying thank you after every sentence, which would be deafening, only people who missed something speak up. You are promised either the whole story or a clear signal that a piece is gone for good.

sections.title: Sources, Receivers and Network Elements
sections.content:
PGM runs over a datagram multicast protocol such as IP multicast, and over IP its protocol number is 113. Three roles take part: sources send data, receivers consume it, and network elements in between help with reliability. Four basic packet types exist: three flow downstream (SPMs, data, NCFs) and one flows upstream (NAKs).

  • ODATA is original data, multicast by the source.
  • SPM, a source path message, is multicast periodically so network elements learn the path back to the source and receivers learn the transmit window.
  • NAK is a negative acknowledgment, unicast by a receiver toward the source for a missing packet.
  • NCF, a NAK confirmation, is multicast in reply to a NAK.
  • RDATA is repair data, sent by the source or by a designated local repairer.

Every packet carries a transport session identifier (TSI), which must be globally unique. It is the combination of a globally unique source identifier and a source-assigned port. PGM also works when some or all network elements do not know PGM, only with less efficiency. SPMs, NCFs and RDATA over IP MUST carry the IP Router Alert Option so PGM-aware elements can pick them out.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a speaker, listeners, and helpers in between. The speaker sends numbered sentences, and every so often a note saying where the speaker is. Listeners who miss a number ask for it, and helpers pass the request along and say they got it.

sections.title: How Loss Is Detected and Repaired
sections.content:
The source numbers ODATA with a sequence number from a circular space of 0 through 2**32 minus 1. It keeps a transmit window of recently sent data available for repair, and it MUST send within a maximum rate using a token bucket or equivalent. SPMs interleaved with data keep path state current, and when idle the source sends heartbeat SPMs at a decaying rate.

A receiver spots a gap in the sequence, or learns of one from an SPM. It then waits a random back-off interval while listening. If it hears a matching NCF or NAK from someone else, it suppresses its own NAK. Otherwise it unicasts a NAK to the upstream PGM network element and repeats it until a matching NCF arrives. After that it waits for the repair. If the retry limits are exceeded or the window moves past the packet, recovery is cancelled, which signals unrecoverable loss.

Each network element confirms a NAK with an NCF multicast on the interface where it arrived and records repair state. It forwards only the first copy of a NAK upstream, discards duplicates, and later sends the RDATA only on the interfaces that asked. The result is usually a single NAK reaching the source per lost packet. The source also confirms with an NCF before sending RDATA.
sections.plainLanguage: If you miss a number, you wait a tiny random moment in case someone else already asked. If nobody has, you ask the nearest helper, who says got it and passes it up the line. The fix is sent back only to those who asked.

sections.title: Packet Headers
sections.content:
Every PGM packet starts with a transport header right after the network header. The common fields are a source port, a destination port, a type, options, a checksum, a global source ID and a TSDU length. The source port plus the global source ID form the TSI. The RFC recommends the low-order 48 bits of the MD5 signature of the source's DNS name as the global source ID.

In the type field the high-order two bits carry a version, 0x0 here, and the low-order nibble gives the packet type. Values 0x0 to 0x3 are SPM-like, 0x4 to 0x7 are data-like, 0x8 to 0xB are NAK-like, and 0xC to 0xF are receiver-sourced session packets. The SPM type is 0x00.

The checksum is the usual one's complement sum over the whole PGM packet, with no pseudo header, for compatibility with network address translation. It is mandatory on ODATA and RDATA, and an element that modifies a header MUST recompute or clear it.

An SPM adds its own sequence number, the trailing and leading edges of the transmit window, and a path address that each PGM network element rewrites as it forwards the SPM. Options extend the header, are added only by the original transmitter, and are never added or removed by network elements.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet has a label on the front saying who sent it, which conversation it belongs to, what kind of packet it is, and a check number to catch scrambling.

sections.title: Options, Repair Helpers, FEC and Congestion
sections.content:
Options are end-to-end extensions, all of which receivers must interpret and some of which network elements must too. They cover fragmentation, late joining, redirection, session synchronization, termination and reset, forward error correction and congestion reports. Fragmentation lets a source split application data to fit the network layer's MTU. Late joining tells receivers whether they may ask for all available repairs when they first join.

The redirect option lets a designated local repairer (DLR) advertise itself so NAKs go to it instead of the original source, which cuts repair latency.

Appendix A adds forward error correction using Reed Solomon erasure codes. From k data packets the source computes parity packets, and a receiver can rebuild the k data packets from any k of the n packets. Parity can be sent pro-actively, recommended where return channels are impossible or costly, or on demand, recommended for very large groups with uncorrelated loss.

Appendix B says a source MUST implement congestion avoidance and defines network element procedures that feed load reports to the source through an option on NAKs. It does not define how the source adapts its rate.
sections.plainLanguage: Extras let a big message be cut into smaller pieces, let local helpers answer requests so the speaker does not have to, and let the speaker send a few spare puzzle pieces so lost ones can be rebuilt.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Beyond ordinary end-to-end authentication problems, PGM has risks specific to how it builds state. Network elements do not just switch SPMs, NAKs, NCFs and RDATA, they interpret them, so abuse can exhaust CPU and memory or muddle repair state. Short of fully authenticating all neighboring sources, receivers, DLRs and network elements, the RFC says the protocol is not impervious to abuse.

  • False SPMs can make elements mis-direct NAKs, so RDATA does not arrive.
  • False NAKs create spurious repair state that lasts until time-out and could exhaust memory.
  • False NCFs can suspend NAK forwarding too early.
  • False RDATA can tear down legitimate repair state.

Precautions are left outside the spec. They include damping jitter in SPM addresses, extending NAK shedding to control the volume of confirmed NAKs, and a three-way handshake between elements and DLRs.
sections.plainLanguage: Since helpers act on any note they are handed, a prankster could send fake notes and confuse them. The rulebook admits there is no full lock on this yet.

fields.name: Source Port
fields.desc: Random source-chosen port; with the global source ID it forms the TSI.

fields.name: Destination Port
fields.desc: Well-known port of the PGM application.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Two bits of version, then the packet type in the low nibble.

fields.name: Options
fields.desc: Flags showing which options are present and their significance.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: One's complement checksum over the whole PGM packet.

fields.name: Global Source ID
fields.desc: Fixed for the life of the session.

fields.name: TSDU Length
fields.desc: Length in octets of the data excluding the transport header.
